title: Open Problem: m(C_t × C_s) for all t, s
context_text: The symmetric difference of two graphs $(V,E_1)$ and $(V,E_2)$ on the same vertex set is $(V,E_1\oplus E_2)$. For a graph $H$, a connectivity code for $H$ is a collection of spanning subgraphs of $H$ such that the symmetric difference of any two distinct members is a connected spanning subgraph of $H$, and $m(H)$ is the maximum size of a connectivity code for $H$. Here $C_t\times C_s$ is the Cartesian (box) product of two cycles (the $t$ by $s$ torus), which is $4$-regular and $4$-edge-connected. In general $2^{\lfloor k'(H)/2\rfloor}\le m(H)\le 2^{k'(H)}$, where $k'(H)$ is the edge-connectivity (the lower bound via Nash-Williams' tree packing), so $4\le m(C_t\times C_s)\le16$. Equality $m(H)=2^{k'(H)}$ holds for complete graphs and, as shown by Bai, Gao, Ma and Wu (who asked about larger tori), $m(C_3\times C_3)=16$; the authors prove it also holds for every $d$-regular mild expander. On the other hand they show that for $s>(2^t+1)2^{t-1}$ the $(t+1)$-regular, $(t+1)$-edge-connected graph $K_t\times C_s$ has $m\le 2^t$; in particular $m(C_3\times C_s)\le8$ for all $s>36$, which answers the question of Bai et al. but does not determine the exact value; they note that determining $m(C_t\times C_s)$ for all $t,s$ remains open.
notes: PDF source; $\times$ denotes the Cartesian (box) product of graphs. The special case $t=3$ ($K_3=C_3$) is resolved by Proposition 3.2; all other cases remain open.
